# **AXIS & ALLIES GLOBAL 1940 — MOD ECR**

## **Enhanced Competitive Ruleset · Complete Edition v3.0**

August 2026

Based on Axis & Allies Global 1940 Second Edition. Original game © Avalon Hill / Wizards of the Coast.

**NEW IN VERSION 3.0**

This edition converts MOD ECR from a six-sided die (d6) system to a **ten-sided die (d10)** system and rebalances every unit accordingly. It also introduces three new land units, tactical bomber target selection, a pre-game ELO balancing procedure, railroad movement for infantry, a stacking limit on land territories, and the eleven Research and Development breakthroughs (Appendix C).

**Every combat value in this rulebook is a d10 value.** Do not mix values from earlier editions or from the out-of-box game with the values printed here.

# **How to Use This Rulebook**

**Part I** contains the MOD ECR modifications. These supplement and override the out-of-box rules reproduced in Part II. Part I is organised into four sections:

* **Section A — Core Competitive Modifications** (Rules 1–12): fundamental balance changes. Recommended for all games.

* **Section B — Advanced Unit Rules** (Rules 13–20): tactical enhancements to specific units.

* **Section C — The d10 System and Unit Overhaul** (Rules 21–26): the combat system, the unit reference chart, new units, unit abilities and combined arms.

* **Section D — Movement and Deployment** (Rules 27–28): railroad movement and the stacking limit.

**Part II** contains the complete out-of-box rules with all agreed house rules folded in. Apply Part II except where modified by Part I. All die values in Part II have already been converted to d10.

**Appendix A** lists the open points that still need a group decision, together with the value used in this edition. **Appendix B** is a one-page quick reference. **Appendix C** holds the Research and Development breakthrough charts and how each one converts to d10.

## **Design Philosophy**

MOD ECR modifications follow three core principles:

* **Component Compatibility:** No new pieces or materials required beyond ten-sided dice.

* **Strategic Balance:** Eliminate exploits while preserving asymmetry.

* **Tactical Depth:** Add meaningful choices without overwhelming complexity.

## **Rules Conventions**

* **Attack (ATK)** and **Defense (DEF)** values are rolled on a **ten-sided die**. A unit scores a hit when it rolls **equal to or less than** its listed value.

* **Cost** is in IPCs. **Move** is in spaces per turn.

* A dash (–) in a stat column means the unit has no value of that kind and is not placed on the battle strip.

* Rules marked **MODIFICATION FROM OOB** change an existing rule. Rules marked **NEW RULE** add something that does not exist in the out-of-box game.

# **PART I: MOD ECR MODIFICATIONS**

## **Section A — Core Competitive Modifications**

The following modifications address fundamental competitive balance issues. They prevent exploitative strategies while maintaining core gameplay.

### **1\. Modified Order of Play**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

Powers take their turns in this modified sequence instead of the OOB order. This adjustment prevents can-opener strategies while maintaining strategic balance.

| Order | MOD ECR | OOB (Reference) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Germany | Germany |
| 2 | United Kingdom Pacific | Soviet Union |
| 3 | Japan | Japan |
| 4 | United Kingdom Europe | United States |
| 5 | Italy | China |
| 6 | China | United Kingdom |
| 7 | Soviet Union | Italy |
| 8 | United States | ANZAC |
| 9 | France | France |

Positions 2, 4, 6, 7 and 8 differ from OOB rules.

**Rationale**

* Eliminates Italian can-opener attacks against the Soviet Union by moving Italy before the USSR.

* Prevents American can-opener attacks weakening German defenses by moving the US after the UK.

* Provides UK Pacific earlier response capability against Japanese expansion.

* Maintains overall strategic balance while closing exploit opportunities.

### **2\. Victory Token System**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

Instead of instant victory by holding capitals, MOD ECR uses a point-based objectives system over a fixed game length.

**Game Length**

Standard games last 8 complete game rounds. The side with the most victory tokens at the end of the final round wins.

**Victory Token Rules**

* Victory tokens may never be awarded twice for the same objective.

* Victory tokens may never be lost after they have been gained.

* Tokens are awarded immediately when the objective condition is met.

* If the score is tied at game end, the Allies win by attrition.

**Axis Victory Objectives**

* **Supremacy:** Control Washington and/or San Francisco.

* **London:** Control London, and/or convoy disrupt a total of 12 IPCs in one turn from originally owned UK Europe territories during their Convoy Disruptions phase.

* **Sydney:** Control Sydney.

* **Moscow:** Control Moscow.

* **China:** Control all 18 originally controlled Chinese territories.

* **Europe:** Control 7 victory cities on the Europe side of the map.

* **Pacific:** Control all 8 originally American islands.

* **Africa:** Control Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Tobruk, Alexandria, Egypt.

* **Asia:** Control Calcutta, Malaya, Hong Kong, Shanghai.

* **Economy:** Control territories worth a combined 144 IPCs.

**Allied Victory Objectives**

* **Supremacy:** Control Berlin and/or Tokyo.

* **Rome:** Control Rome.

* **China:** Control all 18 originally controlled Chinese territories.

* **Europe:** Liberate Paris.

* **Pacific:** Control all 8 originally Japanese islands.

* **Africa:** Control all non-neutral territories on the African continent.

* **Asia:** Control Calcutta, Malaya, Hong Kong, Shanghai.

* **Occupation:** Control Warsaw and all 3 original pro-Axis neutral territories.

* **Diplomacy:** Control all 8 original pro-Allied neutral territories.

* **Attrition:** If the score is tied at the end of the game, the Allies win automatically.

### **3\. Dutch Territory Rule**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

All originally controlled Dutch territories are treated as territories of an Allied power whose capital has been captured. Allied powers may not take control of Dutch territories unless they are liberated from Axis control.

**What This Means**

* Allied powers cannot move into and collect income from unoccupied Dutch territories.

* Allied powers can only gain control by liberating them from Axis occupation.

* Once liberated, the liberating Allied power gains control and collects income normally.

* Applies to: Sumatra, Java, Celebes, Borneo, Dutch New Guinea.

**Rationale**

Prevents early Allied occupation of valuable Dutch territories without opposition, improving game balance and historical accuracy.

### **4\. UK Pacific Declaration of War**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

The United Kingdom Pacific may not declare war on Japan, or perform an act of war against Japan, until the beginning of their 3rd turn.

**Exception**

If Japan declares war on UK Pacific, the United States, and/or Dutch territories before UK Pacific’s 3rd turn, then UK Pacific and the United States may immediately declare war on Japan at the beginning of their next turns.

**Rationale**

Prevents early UK Pacific aggression that could disrupt game balance. Aligns UK Pacific restrictions with the historical situation and US neutrality rules.

### **5\. American Lend-Lease**

**NEW RULE**

During each Mobilize New Units phase in which the United States is a neutral power, the United Kingdom Europe receives the following units at no cost:

* 1 UK Europe fighter placed in Quebec

* 1 UK Europe destroyer placed in Sea Zone 106

**Important Restrictions**

* These units are only received while the United States remains neutral.

* The fighter must be placed in Quebec.

* The destroyer must be placed in Sea Zone 106\.

* These units are placed during the UK Europe Mobilize New Units phase.

**Rationale**

Represents the historical Lend-Lease program. Helps balance the early European theater by strengthening UK defenses during the critical period before American entry.

### **6\. India Industrial Complex**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

**Setup Change.** United Kingdom Pacific begins the game with a minor industrial complex in India instead of a major industrial complex.

**Automatic Upgrade.** This minor complex automatically upgrades to major at no IPC cost immediately when UK Pacific is at war with Japan. The upgrade occurs at the moment war is declared and is effective immediately.

**Rationale**

Prevents UK Pacific from building large forces in India before war with Japan begins, which could create imbalanced opening strategies. The free upgrade ensures UK Pacific still has full production capability once hostilities commence.

### **7\. Capital Purge Rule**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

When a power captures an enemy capital for the first time in the game, the occupying power receives all IPCs currently in the possession of the defeated power.

### **8\. Siberian and Soviet Far East IPC Value Change**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

Siberia is worth 2 IPCs and Soviet Far East is worth 0 IPCs.

### **9\. Johannisburg**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

Union of South Africa now has a Victory City called “Johannisburg”. This increases the number of Victory Cities on the European side.

### **10\. Saharan Passage**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

The areas of Algeria and French Western Africa are adjacent to each other.

### **11\. Argentinian Political Ruling**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

Argentina is no longer strictly Neutral, but instead a “Pro-Axis” Neutral.

### **12\. ELO Game Balancing**

**NEW RULE**

This rule is applied once, before the game begins, after teams and table allocation have been decided.

**Procedure**

1. Calculate the collective average ELO of each team.

2. Take the difference between the two team averages.

3. For every full increment of **4 ELO points** of difference, the team with the lower average ELO receives **1 IPC** of purchasing power.

4. That team spends the IPCs on units and places them on the board before the game starts, following the normal placement restrictions for that power.

*Example: a difference of 12 ELO gives 12 ÷ 4 \= 3 IPCs. A difference of 15 ELO also gives 3 IPCs — only full increments of 4 count.*

**No Pooling with the Faction Bid**

The ELO IPCs and any IPCs won through faction side-bidding (Axis or Allies) are **two separate pools**. The cost of any single unit must be paid entirely from one pool. The two pools may not be combined to pay for one unit.

*Example: a team has 3 ELO IPCs and a positive bidding outcome of 3 IPCs. They may not buy a submarine (6 IPCs) by combining the pools. They may instead buy, for example, 1 infantry from each pool (3 \+ 3 IPCs).*

**Unspent IPCs from either pool are lost** and are not carried into the treasury.

*Game impact: Low.*

## **Section B — Advanced Unit Rules**

The following rules modify specific unit behaviours to add tactical depth.

### **13\. Mechanized Infantry Enhancement**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

**Pairing Rules.** Each artillery paired 1:1 with a mechanized infantry may move up to 2 spaces in the Noncombat Move phase, provided both units start and end their movement in the same territory.

| Army Composition | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 Artillery \+ 1 Mech Inf. | Both move up to 2 spaces |
| 2 Artillery \+ 1 Mech Inf. | Only 1 Artillery and 1 Mech Inf. move up to 2 spaces. The remaining Artillery moves up to 1 space. |

### **14\. “Their Worth Is Political Gold”**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

* Each sunk capital ship gives the sinking power an immediate boost of 1 IPC per sunk capital ship.

* Only Battleships and Aircraft Carriers are considered capital ships.

### **15\. Destroyer Enhancement — Sea Mines**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

* Each destroyer may, during the Purchase phase, lay 1 sea mine for 2 IPCs in the sea zone it is currently in.

* The sea mine is represented by the nation’s roundel in the sea zone.

* **Restriction 1:** Only 1 sea mine may be present in each sea zone per side (Axis/Allies).

* **Restriction 2:** A nation may have no more sea mines on the board than it has destroyers.

**Sea Mine Effect**

Each time an enemy sea unit makes a combat move or noncombat move into a sea zone containing a sea mine — whether ending its movement there or passing through — the moving player rolls one die. **On a roll of 2 or less**, they must immediately take a hit on a ship of their choosing. On a roll of 3 or more, the mine remains and nothing happens.

### **16\. Strategic Bomber Rules**

**NEW RULE**

**Combat Limitations.** Strategic bombers can only roll dice or be claimed as casualties during the first round of combat. After the first round, surviving bombers are set aside as if they had retreated.

**Undefended Transports.** Strategic bombers no longer auto-kill undefended transports. Instead, roll one die per bomber and kill one transport **per roll of 7 or less**.

**Paratrooper Delivery — Combat Move.** Each strategic bomber may deliver up to 2 infantry as paratroopers without technology. Both bomber and infantry must begin movement in the same territory.

* Must invade with at least 1 land unit per infantry delivered.

* Bombers do not roll combat dice when delivering paratroopers.

* Bombers trigger AAA fire and may be hit — cargo dies if the bomber is hit.

**Paratrooper Delivery — Noncombat Move.** Bombers that did not participate in combat may deliver paratroopers during the Noncombat Move phase.

* The destination must have at least 1 friendly faction land unit per infantry delivered.

* The bomber may land in the destination or continue flying with its remaining movement.

![][image1]

### **17\. Cruiser Enhancement**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

The cruiser’s out-of-box pairing bonus with battleships has been **removed** in this edition — the cruiser’s defense value of 6 in the d10 chart already reflects its improved standing (see Rule 25, Combined Arms).

Cruisers retain their built-in anti-aircraft armament: **Anti-Aircraft Fire ×2** (see Rule 24).

| Scenario | Anti-Aircraft shots |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 destroyer and 1 fighter attack 1 cruiser | 1 anti-aircraft roll is made by the defender before the battle |
| 1 fighter and 1 tactical bomber attack 1 cruiser | 2 anti-aircraft rolls are made by the defender before the battle |
| 1 cruiser, 2 fighters and 2 tactical bombers attack 2 cruisers and 1 scrambling fighter | 4 anti-aircraft rolls are made by the defender; 0 for the attacker (attacking cruisers never make anti-aircraft rolls) |

### **18\. Fighter Enhancement**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

* Fighter attack and defense values are set by the unit reference chart (ATK 4 / DEF 5). The separate “fighters defend at 3” adjustment from earlier editions is withdrawn.

* Fighters have the **Interceptor** ability in all combats, with the capability of hitting other aircraft, not only when defending against tactical or strategic bombing raids. See Rule 24\.

### **19\. Naval Blockade System**

**NEW RULE**

**Blockade Basics.** Each defending surface warship can block the movement of up to 3 enemy warships. When attempting to pass through a blockade, the moving player must leave at least 3 warships behind for each blockading surface vessel.

**Screening Force Rules**

* Submarines cannot be included in the screening force unless the blockade includes a destroyer.

* If there are no destroyers in the blockade, submarines slip through automatically.

* The moving player may declare attacks beyond the blockade, but they only occur if the screening force wins.

**Transport Escort Requirements.** To send transports past a blockade, at least one surface warship must remain to escort after accounting for screening requirements.

| Blocking Force | Required to Screen | With Transport |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 Destroyer | 3 warships | 4 warships total |
| 2 Cruisers | 6 warships | 7 warships total |
| 1 Battleship \+ 1 Destroyer | 6 warships | 7 warships total |
| 2 Submarines (no DD) | Your subs slip through | Need 1 warship for escort |

### **20\. Technology Research System**

**NEW RULE**

**Additional Setup Before the Game Begins**

Each **Major power** — Germany, the Soviet Union, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States — chooses a technology and places its roundel upside down in **Phase 1, free of charge**.

**Minor powers** — Italy, UK Pacific, China and France — must wait until their own turn to invest in Research and Development if they wish to.

**The Research Track**

| Step | Cost | Notes |
| :---: | :---- | :---- |
| Entry | 4 IPCs | Pay and place your tech token in Phase 1\. Choose the technology secretly |
| P-1 → P-2 | 4 IPCs | Advance one phase |
| P-2 → P-3 | 4 IPCs | Advance one phase |
| P-3 | **ROLL** | Roll one d6 and pay the amount rolled |
| H (hold) | 1 IPC per die | Buy as many dice as you like; success on 3 or less |

**The P-3 Roll.** Roll **one d6** and pay the amount rolled.

* **If a 6 is rolled,** the advancement takes effect immediately — turn the marker over and place it in an empty slot. The technology is yours.

* **Otherwise,** move the marker to **“H”**. On each following turn you may purchase as many dice as you want for **1 IPC each**, in the hope of rolling a success.

**Discovery Rolls at H.** Each die purchased is a **d6** and succeeds on a roll of **5 or 6**. If any die succeeds, you immediately discover the technology. If all of them fail, they are wasted — you remain at H and try again next turn.

**Restrictions**

* **Only one technology may be in development at any time.**

* **Development may be abandoned at any time, with all investment lost.**

* Once a technology has been discovered, you may begin a new one from the entry step.

* The technology is chosen secretly and is not revealed until first use.

**Note on the P-3 roll.** This roll sets a *price*, not a hit, so it remains a **d6**. The discovery dice at H are d10. See Rule 21, “Which dice stay d6”.

**The eleven available technologies, their effects and their d10 conversions are listed in Appendix C: Research and Development — Breakthrough Charts.**

## **Section C — The d10 System and Unit Overhaul**

### **21\. The d10 Combat System**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

MOD ECR is played with **ten-sided dice**. All attack and defense values, and all rolls that determine whether a hit is scored, are rolled on a d10.

**Why**

The six-sided system forced infantry cost and combat power into a very narrow band, which made infantry-spam the dominant purchase and left the three aircraft types poorly differentiated. The d10 scale gives enough resolution to price infantry honestly against artillery and armour, and to give each aircraft type a distinct role rather than a slightly different number.

The stats in this section are based on *Axis & Allies North Africa*, with modifications — chiefly to sea unit costs, since North Africa has no naval units.

**Reading a value.** A unit scores a hit when it rolls **equal to or less than** its attack value (attacking) or defense value (defending). An infantry defending at 2 hits on a roll of 1 or 2 — a 20% chance.

**Which dice stay d6**

The d10 conversion applies to **hit rolls** only. Three rolls in this rulebook measure a *quantity* rather than a hit, and they remain **six-sided**:

| Roll | Die | Where |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Strategic and tactical bombing damage | **d6** (+2 for strategic bombers) | Phase 4 — Bombing Damage |
| Convoy disruption | **d6** per enemy ship | Phase 8 — Convoy Disruptions |
| Technology P-3 advancement cost | **d6** | Rule 20 |

Every other die roll in this rulebook is a **d10**.

**Converted hit rolls at a glance**

| Roll | Old (d6) | New (d10) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Kamikaze strike | 2 or less | **3 or less** |
| Attacking submarine Surprise Strike | 2 or less | **4 or less** (the submarine’s attack value) |
| Defending submarine Surprise Strike | 1 | **2 or less** (the submarine’s defense value) |
| AAA / Anti-Aircraft Fire | 1 | **1** — unchanged |
| Fighter Interceptor shot | — | **1** |
| Battleship naval bombardment | 4 or less | **7 or less** (the battleship’s attack value) |
| Cruiser naval bombardment | 3 or less | **5 or less** (the cruiser’s attack value) |
| Facility antiaircraft fire vs bombers | 1 | **1** — unchanged |
| Sea mine detonation | 1 | **2 or less** |
| Strategic bomber vs undefended transport | 4 or less | **7 or less** |
| Air battle (escorts vs interceptors) | 1 | **1** — unchanged |
| Technology discovery roll at H | 5 or 6 | **3 or less** |
| Tactical bomber Targeted Attack | — | **4 or less** |

*Game impact: High. This is the largest single change in MOD ECR, but it has been playtested to the point where the obvious pitfalls have already been tuned out.*

* A power that has discovered **Improved Shipyards** buys sea units at the reduced costs in Appendix C.

### **23\. New Units**

**NEW RULE**

Three land units are added to the mobilization chart. They are purchased and mobilized like any other land unit, at any industrial complex you control.

#### *Anti-Tank Gun — 4 IPCs, ATK 2, DEF 3, Move 1*

A cheap defensive specialist. It has the **Anti-Tank** ability (see Rule 24\) in every round of combat, attacking and defending.

#### *Mechanized Anti-Tank Gun — 5 IPCs, ATK 3, DEF 5, Move 2*

A mobile anti-tank platform with a strong defense value. Its **Anti-Tank** ability applies **only in the first round of combat**; from the second round onward its hits are assigned normally.

The Mechanized Anti-Tank Gun **cannot blitz** and does not pair with tanks for blitzing.

#### *Truck — 2 IPCs, no combat value, Move 2*

A logistics unit with no attack or defense value. It is never placed on the battle strip.

**Truck Transport**

* During the **Noncombat Move phase only**, a truck may carry up to **3 infantry**.

* Infantry loaded onto a truck move with the truck, up to the truck’s 2 spaces, and are unloaded at the end of that move.

* Loading and unloading both happen within the same Noncombat Move phase. Infantry carried by a truck may not have moved earlier in the turn, and may not move again after being unloaded.

* Trucks may not carry any unit other than infantry, may not be used during the Combat Move phase, and may not carry units into a hostile territory.

* Trucks may not be loaded onto transports together with their cargo — a truck loaded on a transport is cargo itself, and its own cargo must be unloaded first.

* Trucks are **exempt from the stacking limit** (see Rule 28).

### **24\. Unit Abilities**

**NEW RULE — reference section**

This section defines every ability named in the unit reference chart.

**Anti-Tank.** When a unit with Anti-Tank scores a hit, the opposing player must assign that hit to a **Tank, Mechanized Infantry or Mechanized Anti-Tank Gun** if any is present in the battle. If no such unit is present, the hit is assigned normally. The Mechanized Anti-Tank Gun has this ability in the first round of combat only.

**Anti-Aircraft Fire ×N.** Before the first round of combat, the unit rolls up to **N** dice against attacking air units — one die per attacking air unit, to a maximum of N dice. Each roll of **1** destroys one attacking air unit of the opposing player’s choice. *Anti-aircraft fire keeps its out-of-box hit number of 1 under the d10 system — it is not converted upwards.* Destroyed aircraft are removed before any combat rolls and do not fire.

* Anti-Aircraft Artillery has Anti-Aircraft Fire ×3. It has no attack or defense value and is not placed on the battle strip.

* Cruisers have Anti-Aircraft Fire ×2 in addition to their normal combat values.

* Anti-Aircraft Fire is made by the **defender only**. Attacking AAA and attacking cruisers do not fire.

* Facilities (industrial complexes, air bases, naval bases) have their own antiaircraft systems against bombing raids — see Phase 4\. Do not roll AAA units for bombing raids.

**Interceptor (hits on 1).** In **any** combat — not only when defending against a bombing raid — each fighter may fire one interception shot at enemy **air units** before the first round of combat. Each roll of **1** destroys one enemy air unit of the opposing player’s choice. A fighter that fires an interception shot still fires normally in the combat rounds.

**Targeted Attack.** The tactical bomber’s ability to nominate what it shoots at. See Rule 26\.

**Transport Plane.** The strategic bomber’s paratrooper delivery. See Rule 16\.

**Strategic Bombing Raid.** The strategic bomber may bomb industrial complexes, air bases and naval bases. Tactical bombers may bomb air bases and naval bases but not industrial complexes. See Phase 4\.

**Blitz.** A tank or mechanized infantry may move through an unoccupied hostile territory as the first part of a move. See Phase 3\.

**Supported by Artillery.** A mechanized infantry paired 1:1 with an artillery attacks at **3** instead of 2\.

**Defense Boost.** Each defending Artillery or Tank raises the defense value of up to **2** defending Infantry from 2 to **3**. Each Artillery or Tank may boost at most 2 infantry, and each infantry may be boosted only once. Artillery and Tanks do not boost each other, and do not boost Mechanized Infantry.

**Capital Ship.** Battleships and Aircraft Carriers absorb two hits. The first hit turns the ship on its side (damaged); the second destroys it. Damaged capital ships are repaired at no cost in a sea zone serviced by an operative friendly naval base.

**Naval Bombardment.** Battleships and cruisers may bombard a coastal territory during an amphibious assault. Battleships hit on **7 or less**, cruisers on **5 or less**. See Phase 4\.

**Anti-Submarine Vessel.** A destroyer cancels the Surprise Strike and submerge abilities of enemy submarines in the same battle, and allows friendly air units to hit submarines.

**Sea Mine.** A destroyer may lay a sea mine. See Rule 15\.

**Surprise Strike.** Attacking submarines fire before the main combat rounds, hitting on **4 or less**; defending submarines hit on **2 or less**. See Phase 4, Step 3\.

### **25\. Combined Arms — Revised**

**MODIFICATION FROM OOB**

The d10 rebalancing makes four earlier combined arms bonuses redundant and adds a new defensive one. The complete list of combined arms effects is now:

| Unit Combination | Effect |
| :---- | :---- |
| Infantry \+ Artillery (defending) | Up to 2 Infantry per Artillery defend @ 3 |
| Infantry \+ Tank (defending) | Up to 2 Infantry per Tank defend @ 3 |
| Mech. Infantry \+ Artillery | Mech. Infantry attacks @ 3 |
| Mech. Infantry \+ Tank | Mech. Infantry can blitz |
| Artillery \+ Mech. Infantry | Artillery moves 2 in Noncombat Move (Rule 13\) |
| Plane \+ Destroyer | Plane can hit submarines |

**Withdrawn from OOB and earlier MOD ECR editions**

| Withdrawn Combination | Why |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tactical Bomber \+ Tank | The tactical bomber attacks at 5 in all cases and now has Targeted Attack instead |
| Tactical Bomber \+ Fighter | As above |
| Cruiser \+ Battleship | The cruiser defends at 6 in all cases |
| Infantry \+ Artillery (attacking) | Infantry attacks at 2 in all cases; artillery support is now a defensive bonus |

**Pairing principle (unchanged).** Some unit types require one-to-one pairing with another unit type and may be paired with more than one other unit type. Each unit may be paired with only one other unit at the same time, but may be paired with different units at different times during the same turn. For example, a mechanized infantry may be paired with a tank during the Combat Move phase in order to blitz, and then be paired with an artillery in the Conduct Combat phase in order to attack at 3\.

### **26\. Tactical Bomber — Targeted Attack**

**NEW RULE**

A tactical bomber may forgo its normal attack in order to choose what it hits.

**Procedure**

1. Before the first round of combat, and before any dice are rolled, the attacking player declares for each tactical bomber whether it is making a **normal attack** (ATK 5\) or a **Targeted Attack**.

2. For each tactical bomber making a Targeted Attack, the attacker names one **target category** — a single unit type present in the battle (for example “tanks”, “battleships”, “submarines”).

3. Targeted Attacks are resolved with a **fixed accuracy of 4**: each such tactical bomber hits on a roll of **4 or less**, regardless of its printed attack value and regardless of any other modifier.

4. The defender allocates each hit to a unit **within the named category**.

5. **Excess hits are disregarded.** If more hits are scored against a category than there are units in it, the surplus hits are lost — they may not be reassigned to other units.

**Restriction — transports**

A tactical bomber may not name **transports** as its target category unless there are no other ships or aircraft present in the battle.

**Notes**

* A tactical bomber making a Targeted Attack fires in the normal attacking-units step, not before it.

* Each tactical bomber names its own category; several bombers may name the same category or different ones.

* The choice is made per combat, not per round, and may not be changed once dice are rolled.

*Game impact: Medium.*

## **Section D — Movement and Deployment**

### **27\. Railroad Movement for Infantry**

**NEW RULE**

Territories with a major industrial complex are assumed to sit on a developed rail network.

**The Rule**

From every territory containing a **major industrial complex**, a number of infantry equal to that territory’s **IPC value** gain **\+1 movement** during the **Noncombat Move phase**. Those infantry move 2 spaces instead of 1\.

**Conditions**

* The infantry must **begin** their Noncombat Move in the territory containing the major industrial complex.

* The number of infantry that may use railroad movement each turn is capped at the territory’s printed IPC value. *Example: a major industrial complex on a 5-IPC territory lets up to 5 infantry move 2 spaces that phase.*

* Railroad movement applies to **infantry only** — not artillery, anti-tank guns, AAA or any other land unit.

* Railroad movement applies in the **Noncombat Move phase only**. It never allows an infantry to make a 2-space combat move.

* All other noncombat movement restrictions still apply: the infantry may not move into or through hostile or neutral territories.

* Minor industrial complexes grant no railroad movement.

* Railroad movement and truck transport may not be combined on the same infantry in the same turn.

*Game impact: Low.*

### **28\. Stacking Limit**

**NEW RULE**

Each **land** territory has a maximum number of units that may occupy it.

**The Limit**

**Stacking limit \= 10 \+ the territory’s IPC value.**

*Examples: Japan (8 IPCs) has a limit of 18\. Vyborg (0 IPCs) has a limit of 10\. A 3-IPC territory has a limit of 13\.*

**Exempt Units**

The following do not count towards the stacking limit:

1. Anti-Aircraft Artillery

2. Trucks

3. **Attacking** aircraft

All other units count, including defending and based aircraft, and including units belonging to allied powers sharing the territory.

**When the Limit Is Checked**

The limit is checked at the end of each of the following phases, and any excess must be resolved before the phase ends:

* End of the **Combat Move** phase — you may not move units into a territory beyond its limit.

* End of the **Noncombat Move** phase — you may not move or land units into a territory beyond its limit.

* End of the **Mobilize New Units** phase — you may not place new units in a territory beyond its limit.

**Clarifications**

* The limit applies to **land territories only**. Sea zones have no stacking limit.

* Attacking aircraft are exempt while the battle is being fought. Once combat is over, surviving air units must land in the Noncombat Move phase in a territory that is within its limit — if no legal landing space exists, the air unit is lost as normal.

* Units in transit — passing through a territory without ending their movement there — do not count.

**Rationale**

This prevents a single territory on a front from absorbing an entire army as a “death ball”. Broadening a front now requires mobility, or investment in airpower to deliver heavier attacks from outside the stack.

*Game impact: Medium.*

# **PART II: STANDARD RULES (d10 CONVERTED)**

Complete out-of-box rules plus agreed house rules follow. Apply except where modified by MOD ECR in Part I. All die values below have been converted to d10 except the three magnitude rolls listed in Rule 21\.

*Note: UK Pacific (formerly ANZAC) references should be read as UK Pacific per MOD ECR.*

## **Spaces on the Game Board**

### **Territories**

The border colours of the territories on the game board show which power controls them at the start of the game. Each power has its own colour and emblem (the United Kingdom controls the Canadian territories in addition to those with its own emblem). When the rules refer to the “original controller” of a territory, they mean the power whose emblem is printed on the territory.

Most territories have an income value ranging from 1 to 10\. This is the number of IPCs the territory produces each turn for its controller. A few territories, such as Wake Island, have no income value.

Units can move between adjacent spaces (those that share a common border). Spaces that meet only at a point are not adjacent to one another.

All territories exist in one of three conditions:

* **Friendly:** Controlled by you or a friendly power.

* **Hostile:** Controlled by an enemy power (a power with which you are at war).

* **Neutral:** Not controlled by any power, or controlled by a power on the other side with which you are not yet at war. Neutral territories have white borders and no power’s emblem. Most such territories also have a unit silhouette with a number, which indicates how many infantry units the territory will generate to defend itself when its neutrality is violated. The Himalayas, the Sahara Desert and the Pripet Marshes are impassable and may not be moved into or through by any units.

### **Sea Zones**

Sea zones are either friendly or hostile. Friendly sea zones contain no surface warships (this does not include submarines and transports) belonging to a power with which you are at war. Hostile sea zones contain surface warships belonging to a power with which you are at war. The presence of a surface warship belonging to a power on the other side with which you are not yet at war does not make a sea zone hostile.

*Note: The Caspian Sea (surrounded by Caucasus, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Eastern Persia, Persia and Northwest Persia) is considered to be a sea zone, even though it does not have a number.*

### **Islands**

An island or island group is a single territory surrounded entirely by one or more sea zones. A sea zone can contain at most one island or island group, which is considered one territory. It is not possible to split up land-based units so that they are on different islands in the same group.

For example, Sardinia and Sicily are both located in sea zone 95\. These named islands can each have independent land-based units. However, West Indies, located in sea zone 89, is an island group (one territory), so any land units there are all together. Islands that have no name label, such as the one in sea zone 1, are not game spaces and may not have units moved onto them.

### **Canals and Narrow Straits**

Canals are artificial waterways that connect two larger bodies of water; narrow straits are natural passages that do the same. In either case, control of the land territories surrounding these features gives the controlling power and its allies the ability to travel through them while denying access to enemy powers.

There are two canals on the game board. The Panama Canal connects sea zones 64 and 89; the Suez Canal connects sea zones 81 and 98\. A canal is not considered a space, so it does not block land movement.

There are three narrow straits. The Turkish Straits connect sea zones 99 and 100, the Strait of Gibraltar connects sea zones 91 and 92, and the Danish Straits connect sea zones 112 and 113\. Narrow straits cannot be crossed by land units without the use of transport ships.

| Canal / Strait | Controlling Territories |
| :---- | :---- |
| Suez Canal | Egypt and Trans-Jordan |
| Panama Canal | Central America |
| Turkish Straits | Turkey |
| Strait of Gibraltar | Gibraltar |
| Danish Straits | Denmark |

If there is only one controlling territory, the power that controls it controls the canal or strait. If there are two controlling territories, the side that controls both of them controls the canal or strait. If one side controls one territory and the other controls the other, the canal or strait is closed to sea units.

Submarines of any power may pass through the Strait of Gibraltar regardless of which power controls it. The movement of air units is completely unaffected by canals and straits.

## **Setup**

Link the western edge of the Pacific 1940 map with the eastern edge of the Europe 1940 map. The combined board wraps around horizontally.

Set up units as shown on the setup charts found in Pacific 1940 and Europe 1940\. Additionally, place the following units:

* **Amur:** 6 Soviet Infantry

* **Sakha:** 6 Soviet Infantry and 2 Soviet AAA

* **Buryatia:** 6 Soviet Infantry

* **Egypt:** 2 UK Pacific Infantry (also, remove 1 United Kingdom infantry)

Then apply the ELO balancing procedure in Rule 12 and any faction side-bid before the first turn begins.

**Free technology roundel.** Each Major power — Germany, the Soviet Union, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States — chooses a technology and places its roundel upside down in Phase 1, free of charge. Minor powers (Italy, UK Pacific, China and France) must wait until their own turn to invest in Research and Development. See Rule 20\.

**Starting IPC Income Levels and Treasuries**

| Power | Starting Income |
| :---- | :---- |
| Germany | 30 |
| Soviet Union | 37 |
| Japan | 26 |
| United States | 52 |
| China | 12 |
| United Kingdom – Europe | 28 |
| United Kingdom – Pacific | 27 |
| Italy | 10 |
| France | 19 |

## **Order of Play**

Your power’s turn consists of eight phases, which take place in a fixed sequence. You must collect income if you can, but all other parts of the turn sequence are voluntary.

**Turn Sequence**

1. Research and Development

2. Purchase and Repair Units

3. Combat Move (Powers at War only)

4. Conduct Combat (Powers at War only)

5. Noncombat Move

6. Mobilize New Units

7. Collect Income

8. Convoy Disruptions against the current power’s turn

Powers take their turns in the MOD ECR order given in Rule 1\.

## **PHASE 1: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT**

In this phase you may invest in Research and Development. The full procedure — entry cost, the P-1 and P-2 advancement costs, the P-3 roll and the discovery dice at H — is given in **Rule 20**. The eleven technologies and their effects are in **Appendix C**.

* Only one technology may be in development at any time.

* Development may be abandoned at any time, with all investment lost.

* Major powers begin the game with a free technology roundel already placed in Phase 1 (see Rule 20). Minor powers must wait until their own turn to invest.

A technology discovered in this phase is in effect for the rest of this turn.

## **PHASE 2: PURCHASE AND REPAIR UNITS**

In this phase you may spend IPCs on units to be used in future turns. All the units listed in the mobilization zone on the game board are available for purchase by all powers, at the costs given in Rule 22\.

**Purchase Units Sequence**

1. Order units.

2. Pay for units and repair damaged units and facilities.

3. Place units in the mobilization zone.

**Step 1: Order Units.** You may purchase as many units of any type as you can afford and will have the ability to mobilize (see Phase 6\) after making repairs to any damaged industrial complexes. You do not have to spend all of your IPCs. The number of pieces in play is not limited by the number of plastic and cardboard pieces available.

**Step 2: Pay for Units and Repair Damaged Units and Facilities.** Pay IPCs to the bank equal to the total cost of the units. You can also pay to remove damage from facilities. Each point of damage costs 1 IPC to remove. Repairs take effect immediately. Your capital ships (carriers and battleships) in sea zones serviced by operative friendly naval bases are also repaired at this time at no IPC cost.

Sea mines are also purchased during this phase (see Rule 15).

**Step 3: Place Units in the Mobilization Zone.** Place the purchased units in the mobilization zone. You cannot use these units right away, but you will deploy them later in the turn.

### **Declaring War**

If there are no restrictions currently keeping you from being at war with a power on the other side, you may declare war on that power. War must be declared on your turn at the beginning of the Combat Move phase, before any combat movements are made, unless otherwise specified in the political rules. An actual attack is not required.

Once a state of war is entered into, all territories and sea zones controlled by or containing units belonging to the power on which you declared war instantly become hostile to your units, with one exception: during your Combat Move phase in which you entered into a state of war, your transports that are already in sea zones that have just become hostile may be loaded in those sea zones.

Declarations of war are either ‘provoked’ or ‘unprovoked’. A declaration of war is considered provoked either when it is made in reaction to the direct aggression of another power, or when a political rule allows the power to declare war due to a specific action taken by another power.

## **PHASE 3: COMBAT MOVE (Powers at War Only)**

Movement is separated into combat movement and noncombat movement. During the Combat Move phase, all movement must end in a hostile space, with a few exceptions. Movement into a hostile space counts as combat movement whether that space is occupied or not.

Move as many of your units into as many hostile territories and sea zones as you wish. You can move into a single hostile space from different spaces, as long as each moving unit can reach that space with a legal move.

**The stacking limit (Rule 28\) applies at the end of this phase.**

### **Exceptions to Ending Movement in Hostile Spaces**

You can move units through friendly (but not friendly neutral) spaces en route to hostile spaces. However, units can’t end their movement in friendly spaces during the Combat Move phase except in four instances:

1. Tanks and mechanized infantry that have blitzed through an unoccupied hostile space.

2. Units moving from an enemy-occupied sea zone to escape combat as their combat move. A sea zone into which defending air units may be scrambled in reaction to an amphibious assault may be treated in the same way for this purpose.

3. Sea units that will be participating in an amphibious assault from a friendly sea zone, as well as sea and/or air units that may be needed to support it in case defending air units are scrambled.

4. Units moving into a sea zone containing only enemy submarines and/or transports in order to attack those units.

### **General Combat Movement Rules**

If you move all of your units out of a territory you control, you still retain control of that territory until an enemy moves into and captures it.

Units from the same side can freely share territories and space on aircraft carriers and transports with one another, as long as both powers are at war. They may share sea zones regardless of their status. These shared events must be agreed upon by both powers. **Allied units sharing a land territory count towards that territory’s stacking limit.**

All combat movement is considered to take place at the same time. You cannot move a unit, then conduct combat, then move that unit again during this phase. The only exception is land units making an amphibious assault preceded by a sea battle. You can’t move additional units into an embattled space once an attack has begun.

A land or sea unit can move a number of spaces up to its move value. Most units must stop when they enter a hostile space.

Enemy submarines and/or transports don’t block any of your units’ movement, nor do they prevent loading or offloading in that sea zone. As the moving player, you have the option of attacking any enemy submarines and/or transports that share a sea zone with you. However, if a unit chooses to make such an attack, that unit must end its movement in that sea zone, and it must attack all such units present.

### **Sea Units Starting in Enemy-Occupied Sea Zones**

If your units are sharing a sea zone with only enemy submarines and/or transports and you want to ignore them, the normal rules of combat movement apply. However, if they are sharing a sea zone with enemy surface warships, or you are attacking enemy submarines and/or transports there, each of your units must do one of the following:

1. Remain in the sea zone and conduct combat;

2. Leave the sea zone, load units if desired, and conduct combat elsewhere;

3. Leave the sea zone, either to load units or to establish a retreat route, and return to the same sea zone to conduct combat; or

4. Leave the sea zone and conduct no combat.

You can only load units in friendly sea zones. Once these sea units have moved and/or participated in combat, they can’t move or participate in the Noncombat Move phase of the turn.

### **Air Units**

An air unit that moves in the Combat Move phase must generally reserve part of its move value for the Noncombat Move phase, at which point it must return to a safe landing spot using its remaining movement.

An air unit’s movement in any complete turn is limited to its total move value. A strategic bomber with a move value of 6 can’t move 6 spaces to get to a hostile space — it must save enough movement to reach a friendly territory where it can land. A fighter or tactical bomber can move its full 4 spaces to attack in a sea zone instead of saving movement, but only if a carrier could be there for it to land on by the conclusion of the Mobilize New Units phase.

**Attacking aircraft are exempt from the stacking limit during the attack, but must land in a territory that is within its limit (Rule 28).**

### **Declaring Bomber Targets**

If bombers (strategic or tactical) are moving into territories containing both combat units and facilities, it must be declared which bombers are attacking the combat units and which are attacking the facilities. Air units attacking combat units in territories that have AAA will be fired upon. This doesn’t include territories containing AAA that are only being flown over. AAA can’t fire upon bombers conducting strategic or tactical bombing raids — those air units are fired on by the antiaircraft cover provided by the industrial complex or base being attacked.

**Tactical bombers must also declare Targeted Attacks at this point if the target category is to be named before scrambling (Rule 26 allows the declaration up to the moment before the first dice are rolled).**

### **Amphibious Assaults**

If you want to make any amphibious assaults, announce your intent to do so during the Combat Move phase. An amphibious assault takes place when you attack a coastal territory or island group from a sea zone by offloading land units from transports into that target territory. The sea zone may be either friendly or hostile, but if it is hostile it must be made friendly through sea combat before the amphibious assault can commence.

Moving transports and their cargo into a sea zone from which you plan to make an amphibious assault counts as a combat move, even if there are no defending surface warships there. This is also true of any units that will support the assault.

During the Conduct Combat phase, you can launch only amphibious assaults that you announced during this phase.

If an amphibious assault involves a sea combat, any air units participating in the assault must move to either the sea zone or the land territory. They will then participate only in the part of the assault to which they have moved.

### **Special Combat Movement**

**Aircraft Carriers.** Although they have an attack value of only 1, carriers can participate in an attack and can take hits. Any fighters or tactical bombers on an aircraft carrier launch before the carrier moves and move independently of the carrier. Guest aircraft belonging to a friendly power on board another power’s carrier must remain on board as cargo if the carrier moves; they can’t take part in combat and are destroyed if the carrier is destroyed. Whether it moves during the Combat Move or Noncombat Move phase, an aircraft carrier allows friendly fighters and tactical bombers to land on it in the sea zone where it finishes its move.

**Submarines.** If there are no enemy destroyers present, a submarine can move through a sea zone containing enemy warships without stopping. However, if a submarine enters a sea zone containing an enemy destroyer during the Combat Move phase, its movement ends immediately and combat will result.

**Tanks, Mechanized Infantry and Blitzing.** A tank can blitz by moving through an unoccupied hostile territory as the first part of a move that can end in a friendly or hostile territory. In addition, 1 mechanized infantry unit can move along with each blitzing tank. The complete move must occur during the Combat Move phase. The blitzing units establish control of the first territory before they move to the next. A tank (or mechanized infantry) that encounters enemy units, including AAA, or an industrial complex, air base or naval base in the first territory it enters must stop there and may not blitz.

*The Mechanized Anti-Tank Gun and the Truck have a move value of 2 but cannot blitz.*

| ✓ You CAN Blitz | ✗ You CANNOT Blitz |
| :---- | :---- |
| Through an unoccupied hostile territory, ending in a friendly or hostile territory | If the first territory contains any enemy units (even AAA) |
| From a friendly territory through one empty hostile territory to another territory | If the first territory contains an industrial complex, air base or naval base |
| With mechanized infantry (one mech per tank) | Through or into neutral territories |

**Transports.** If a transport encounters hostile surface warships after it begins to move (not counting the sea zone it started in), its movement for that turn ends and it must stop there and conduct sea combat.

A transport can load units while in any friendly sea zone along its route, including the sea zone it started in. If a transport loads land units during the Combat Move phase, it must offload those units to attack a hostile territory as part of an amphibious assault during the Conduct Combat phase, or it must retreat during the sea combat step of the amphibious assault sequence. A transport is not allowed to offload land units for an amphibious assault in a sea zone containing 1 or more ignored enemy submarines unless at least 1 warship belonging to the attacking power is also present at the end of the Combat Move phase.

Any land units aboard a transport are considered cargo until they offload. Cargo can’t take part in sea combat and is destroyed if the transport is destroyed.

**Air Bases.** When taking off from a territory that has an operative air base, air units gain 1 additional movement point. Fighters and tactical bombers can move 5 spaces and strategic bombers can move 7 spaces.

**Naval Bases.** All ships beginning their movement from a sea zone serviced by an operative friendly naval base gain 1 additional movement point.

### **Scramble**

Scrambling is a special movement the defender can make at the end of this phase, after all of the attacker’s combat movements have been completed and all attacks have been declared. The attacker may not change any combat movements or attacks after the defender has scrambled.

A quick reaction team of no more than 3 defending fighters and/or tactical bombers (strategic bombers can’t scramble) located on each island or coastal territory that has an operative air base can be scrambled to defend against attacks in the adjacent sea zones. They can also be scrambled to resist amphibious assaults from adjacent sea zones, whether or not the territory being assaulted contains the air base. Air units belonging to powers friendly to the attacked power may be scrambled by their owner if that power is at war with the attacking power, so long as the limit of 3 total air units is respected.

**Multiple Air Bases and Sea Zones.** Where a sea zone is adjacent to more than one territory containing an air base, each of those territories can scramble up to 3 air units. Where a territory containing an air base is adjacent to more than one sea zone, the territory may still only scramble up to 3 air units, but they may be split between the sea zones in any combination.

**Scrambled Unit Behaviour.** Scrambled fighters and tactical bombers are defending, so use their defense values and abilities. Scrambled fighters may make their Interceptor shot. As defenders, they may not retreat. They can’t participate in any other battles during that turn.

After all combat is completed, each surviving scrambled air unit must return to the territory from which it was scrambled. If the enemy has captured that territory, the unit can move 1 space to land in a friendly territory or on a friendly aircraft carrier. If no such landing space is available, the unit is lost.

### **Powers Not at War with One Another**

**Movement.** A power’s ships don’t block the naval movements of other powers with which it’s not at war, and vice versa. They can occupy the same sea zones.

**Combat.** A power can’t attack a territory controlled by or containing units belonging to a power with which it is not at war. If a power at war attacks a sea zone containing units belonging to both a power with which it’s already at war and a power with which it’s not at war, the latter power’s units are ignored.

**The United States Special Restrictions.** The United States begins the game neutral. It may not move land or air units into neutral territories. It may not move units into territories or onto ships belonging to another power or use another power’s naval bases, nor may another power move land or air units into its territories or onto its ships or use its naval bases. In addition, the United States may not end the movement of its sea units in sea zones that are adjacent to Japanese-controlled territories.

### **Quick Reference: Combat Move Phase**

| Action | Key Points |
| :---- | :---- |
| Move Units | All movement must end in hostile spaces (with four exceptions) |
| Declare Attacks | Move units into hostile territories/sea zones; announce amphibious assaults |
| Air Units | Must reserve movement to reach safe landing; declare bomber targets |
| Special Moves | Blitzing tanks, submarine movement, carrier operations, scrambling (defender) |
| Stacking | Check the 10 \+ IPC limit in every land territory at the end of the phase |
| Important | All movement is simultaneous; no adding units once combat begins |

**Movement Restrictions by Unit Type**

| Unit Type | Move | Special Movement Rules |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Infantry | 1 | Stop when entering hostile territory. \+1 in Noncombat Move from a major IC territory (Rule 27). May be carried by a truck in Noncombat Move. |
| Artillery | 1 | May move 2 in Noncombat Move if paired 1:1 with a Mech Infantry starting and ending in the same territory (Rule 13\) |
| Anti-Tank Gun | 1 | Stop when entering hostile territory |
| Mech. Anti-Tank Gun | 2 | Cannot blitz |
| Anti-Aircraft Artillery | 1 | May move only in the Noncombat Move phase |
| Tank | 2 | Can blitz through an unoccupied hostile territory |
| Mech Infantry | 2 | Can blitz with a tank (one mech per tank) |
| Truck | 2 | Noncombat Move only when carrying infantry; may not enter hostile territory |
| Fighters | 4 | 5 from an air base; must reserve movement for landing |
| Tactical Bombers | 4 | 5 from an air base; must reserve movement for landing |
| Strategic Bombers | 6 | 7 from an air base; must reserve movement for landing |
| Sea Units | 2 | 3 from a naval base; stop when entering a hostile sea zone |
| Submarines | 2 | Can move through enemy ships (except destroyers); stop at an enemy destroyer |

### **Common Mistakes and Important Reminders**

* **Movement is permanent.** Once you’ve moved units and announced attacks, you cannot change your mind after the defender has responded.

* **Air units need landing zones.** You must be able to demonstrate a possible landing zone for all air units before rolling any dice, and that landing zone must be within its stacking limit.

* **Transports in amphibious assaults.** Moving transports into position counts as a combat move, even if the sea zone is currently friendly.

* **Scrambling happens last.** The defender decides which aircraft to scramble after all attacker movements are complete.

* **Blitzing restrictions.** Tanks cannot blitz if they encounter ANY enemy units in the first territory, including AAA and facilities.

* **Submarines and destroyers.** Submarines move through enemy fleets freely unless an enemy destroyer is present.

* **Air bases and naval bases** only provide movement bonuses when units START their movement from those locations.

* **Mechanized infantry can only blitz** when paired one-to-one with a tank.

* **Trucks cannot move in the Combat Move phase** while carrying infantry.

## **PHASE 4: CONDUCT COMBAT (Powers at War Only)**

In this phase you conduct combat against opposing units using the following sequence:

1. Strategic and tactical bombing raids

2. Amphibious assaults

3. General combat

A number of units have special rules that modify or overwrite the combat rules in this section. **All combat rolls are made on a d10.**

### **Kamikaze Strikes**

The Japanese player has the ability to make a special defensive strike against Allied surface warships. Japan is allowed to make 6 kamikaze strikes during the game, only in sea zones that contain the Kamikaze symbol: those surrounding Japan, Okinawa, Iwo Jima, Formosa, Marianas and Philippines.

If an Allied player attacks Japanese units in, or declares an amphibious assault from, one of these sea zones, the Japanese player can announce at the beginning of this phase that they intend to launch one or more kamikaze strikes in that sea zone. They are resolved before any combat begins.

The Japanese player must declare how many kamikaze strikes will be made, in which sea zone(s), and which enemy ship will be struck by each kamikaze, before any dice are rolled. For each declared strike, 1 Kamikaze token must be spent and will be removed from the game after the strike is resolved. A kamikaze strike can target any specific enemy surface warship (not a submarine or transport) belonging to the attacking power. More than one kamikaze strike can be made against the same ship.

**Kamikaze strikes hit on a roll of 3 or less.** If a hit is scored, it must be applied to the chosen unit. Surface warships destroyed by a kamikaze strike (capital ships still take 2 hits) are immediately removed and will not participate in the subsequent battle. A kamikaze strike prevents offshore bombardment supporting an amphibious assault in that sea zone, whether or not the strike is successful.

### **Strategic and Tactical Bombing Raids**

A strategic or tactical bombing raid is a direct attack on a facility. During this step, you can bomb enemy industrial complexes, air bases and naval bases with your strategic bombers. You can also bomb enemy air and naval bases (but not industrial complexes) with your tactical bombers.

To conduct a bombing raid, the attacking player moves their bombers to the territory containing the target(s). A base may be both strategically and tactically bombed at the same time. Both attacking and defending fighters (not tactical bombers) can also participate as escorts and interceptors.

**Escort Fighters.** Escort fighters can escort and protect the bombers, and they can originate from any territory or sea zone, range permitting. They can’t participate in any other battles during that turn.

**Interceptor Fighters.** Any number of defending fighters based in a territory that is about to be bombed can be committed to the defense of that territory’s facilities as interceptors, whether or not there are attacking fighter escorts. The number is decided by the owning player(s) after the attacker’s Combat Move phase is completed and before the Conduct Combat phase begins. These fighters cannot participate in other battles during that turn and must remain in their original territory after the battle. If that territory is captured, they can move 1 space to land in a friendly territory or on a friendly aircraft carrier during the Noncombat Move phase.

**Air Battle.** If the defender has committed fighter interceptors, an air battle is fought immediately before the bombing raid. Only one air battle is fought in each territory. It is resolved in the same way as a normal combat, with the following exceptions:

1. The attacking bombers and fighter escorts and the defending fighter interceptors are the only units participating.

2. The combat lasts for only one round.

3. **All air units hit on a roll of 1**, whether attacking or defending.

After the air battle, or if there were no defending interceptors, surviving fighter escorts are considered to have retreated. They don’t participate in the actual bombing raid, are not subject to antiaircraft fire, and remain in the territory until the Noncombat Move phase. Any surviving attacking bombers carry out the bombing raid. If the territory offers more than one target, the bombers may be divided into groups, each assigned a specific target (tactical bombers may not attack industrial complexes).

**Antiaircraft Fire.** Each industrial complex, air base and naval base has its own antiaircraft system. If there is an AAA unit in the targeted territory, don’t roll for it — those units protect combat units. Each complex and base rolls one die against each bomber directly attacking it. **For each roll of 1**, a bomber of the attacker’s choice is immediately removed.

**Bombing Damage.** After resolving antiaircraft fire, surviving bombers each roll **one d6**. Add 2 to each die rolled for a strategic bomber (but not for tactical bombers), then total the result. Place 1 grey plastic chip under the targeted facility per damage point rolled. A major industrial complex can’t receive more than 20 total damage; a minor one no more than 6\. Air bases and naval bases can’t receive more than 6 total damage. Damage exceeding these limits is not applied.

A bomber that performed a bombing raid can’t participate in any other combat this turn and must return to a friendly territory during the Noncombat Move phase.

**Why a d6 here.** The bombing roll measures how much damage is done, not whether a hit lands. Rolling it on a d10 would roughly double average bombing damage against unchanged facility damage caps. It stays a d6 (see Rule 21).

### **Amphibious Assaults**

During this step you resolve each amphibious assault you announced during the Combat Move phase.

**Amphibious Assault Sequence**

1. Sea combat

2. Battleship and cruiser bombardment

3. Land combat

**Step 1: Sea Combat.** If there are defending surface warships and/or scrambled air units, sea combat occurs. If there are only defending submarines and/or transports, the attacker can choose to ignore those units or conduct sea combat. If sea combat occurs, all attacking and defending sea and air units present must participate. Conduct the sea combat using the rules for General Combat, then go to step 3\. If no sea combat occurs, go to step 2\.

**Step 2: Battleship and Cruiser Bombardment.** If there was NOT a combat in the sea zone from which you are offloading units, any accompanying battleships and cruisers in that sea zone can conduct a one-time bombardment of one coastal territory or island group being attacked. The number of ships that can bombard is limited to 1 ship per land unit being offloaded into that coastal territory. If more than one territory is being assaulted from the same sea zone, each ship may support only one assault. Choosing to destroy enemy transports or attacking enemy submarines in step 1 counts as a combat and prevents bombardment.

Roll one die for each battleship and cruiser that can bombard. **Battleships hit on a roll of 7 or less; cruisers hit on a roll of 5 or less.** For each hit, the defender moves a defending unit behind the casualty strip. These casualties will be able to defend during the land combat step before they are eliminated.

**Step 3: Land Combat.** Land combat can only take place if there was no sea battle, or the sea zone has been cleared of all defending enemy units except transports and submerged submarines. Move all attacking and defending units to the battle strip and conduct combat using the General Combat rules. Remember to put casualties from bombardment behind the casualty strip.

Attacking land units can come from transports (seaborne) and from neighbouring territories adjacent to the attacked territory. Any land units offloading from a single transport can only be offloaded into a single hostile territory.

If no land units survived the sea combat, or if the attacking sea units withdrew, then any other units designated to participate in the land attack (including air units) must still conduct one round of land combat before they can retreat.

**Retreat Rules.** Keep the attacking overland units and seaborne land units separated on the battle strip. Attacking seaborne units can’t retreat. Attacking overland land units and air units can retreat between rounds of combat. All attacking overland land units must retreat together as a group, to a territory from which at least one of them entered the contested territory. Attacking air units retreat according to the attacker retreat rules and land during the Noncombat Move phase.

**Air Units.** Each attacking air unit can participate in the sea battle or the attack on the coastal territory, not both. The attacking player must declare which air units are involved in each part of the attack and can’t change their assignments later. At the end of the amphibious assault, all air units remain in place and land during the Noncombat Move phase.

Air units defending in a territory can fight only in that territory and can’t participate in the sea combat. The exception is defending fighters and tactical bombers on an island or coastal territory with an operative air base, which can be scrambled.

### **General Combat**

In this step you resolve combat in each space that contains your units and either contains enemy units or is enemy-controlled. Combat in each space takes place at the same time, but each affected space is resolved separately and completely before resolving the next. The attacker decides the order. No new units can enter as reinforcements once combat has begun.

If you moved units into unoccupied hostile territories, or hostile territories containing only facilities and/or AAA units, no actual combat is necessary (though AAA units will still fire at attacking air units). Skip to step 7 for each of these territories and remove any AAA units in them.

**General Combat Sequence**

1. Place units along the battle strip

2. Pre-combat fire: Anti-Aircraft Fire and Interceptor shots

3. Submarine Surprise Strike or submerge (sea battles only)

4. Attacking units fire

5. Defending units fire

6. Remove defender’s casualties

7. Press attack or retreat

8. Conclude combat

#### *Step 1: Place Units Along the Battle Strip*

Place all attacking and defending land, sea and air units from the battle onto their respective sides of the strip, using the values in the Unit Reference Chart (Rule 22). An attacking or defending unit must roll its attack or defense value **or less on a d10** in order to score a hit.

Some units — transports, AAA and trucks — have no combat value and are not represented on the battle strip. Place these units beside the strip; they are still participants and may be taken as casualties.

In a sea battle, place any cargo beside the transport or on the aircraft carrier that is carrying it. Cargo doesn’t roll for hits, nor can it be chosen as a casualty. It’s lost with the ship carrying it.

If you are attacking in a sea zone that already contained friendly units, your ally’s units are not placed along the battle strip but remain out of play for this turn.

**Combined Arms.** See Rule 25 for the complete list of combined arms effects under the d10 system.

#### *Step 2: Pre-Combat Fire*

Before the first round of combat only, and in this order:

1. **Anti-Aircraft Fire.** The defender rolls for each Anti-Aircraft Artillery (×3) and each cruiser (×2) present, up to one die per attacking air unit. Each roll of **1** destroys one attacking air unit of the attacker’s choice. Only the defender fires.

2. **Interceptor shots.** Each fighter on either side may fire one shot at enemy air units, hitting on a roll of **1**. Attacker rolls first, then defender. Destroyed air units are removed and do not fire.

Aircraft destroyed in this step do not participate in the combat.

#### *Step 3: Submarine Surprise Strike or Submerge (Sea Battles Only)*

Before the general sea battle takes place, both attacking and defending submarines can choose to either make a Surprise Strike roll or submerge. A player may submerge all, some or none of their submarines. However, if the opposing side has a destroyer in the battle, the submarines can’t submerge or make a Surprise Strike — combat proceeds normally with the submarines firing along with the other units.

Attacking or defending submarines that submerge are immediately removed from the battle strip and returned to the contested sea zone.

*Decisions on whether submarines will fire or submerge must be made before any dice are rolled by either side. The attacking player decides first.*

**Each attacking submarine conducting a Surprise Strike rolls one die and scores a hit on a roll of 4 or less.** The defender then chooses 1 sea unit (submarines can’t hit air units) for each hit scored and moves it behind the casualty strip.

**Then each defending submarine conducting a Surprise Strike rolls one die and scores a hit on a roll of 2 or less.** The attacker chooses 1 sea unit for each hit scored and removes it from play.

In both cases, transports can be chosen as casualties only if there are no other eligible units. Submerged submarines can’t be chosen as casualties. Undamaged capital ships hit only once are not removed.

Once all Surprise Strikes have been made, the casualties they generated are removed. As long as there are submarines and no opposing destroyers, this step is repeated each round of combat.

#### *Step 4: Attacking Units Fire*

Roll one die for each attacking unit with an attack value that didn’t fire or submerge in step 3\. Roll for units with the same attack value at the same time. An attacking unit scores a hit if you roll its attack value **or less**.

Tactical bombers making a Targeted Attack (Rule 26\) fire in this step, hitting on **4 or less**, and their hits are allocated within the named category.

Hits from units with **Anti-Tank** must be assigned to a Tank, Mechanized Infantry or Mechanized Anti-Tank Gun if any is present.

After the attacking player has rolled for all attacking units, the defender chooses 1 unit for each remaining hit and moves it behind the casualty strip. All units behind the casualty strip will return fire in step 5\. As many hits as possible must be assigned. For instance, if 1 cruiser and 2 submarines attack a carrier with a fighter and score 3 hits, the defender must assign the cruiser hit to the fighter and the submarine hits to the carrier.

#### *Step 5: Defending Units Fire*

Defending units roll one die for each unit with a defense value, including units behind the casualty strip, that didn’t fire or submerge in step 3\. A defending unit scores a hit if you roll its defense value **or less**. Defending infantry use their boosted value of 3 where a defending Artillery or Tank supports them (Rule 24).

After the defending player has rolled, the attacker chooses 1 unit for each hit scored and removes it from play. As many hits as possible must be assigned.

**Specific to sea battles:** submarines that fired in step 3 can’t fire again during the same combat round. If there is an enemy destroyer in the battle, submarines fire in step 4 or 5 rather than step 3\. Hits from air units can’t be assigned to submarines unless there is a destroyer friendly to the air units in the battle, and hits can only be assigned to transports if there are no other eligible units.

**Defenseless Transports.** In a sea battle, if the defender has only transports remaining and the attacker still has units capable of attacking, the defending transports are all destroyed along with their cargo. This also occurs if the only combat units remaining can’t hit each other. Attacking transports are not usually considered defenseless, since they generally have the option of retreating; if they can’t retreat, they are treated the same as defending transports.

*Strategic bombers attacking undefended transports do not auto-kill them — see Rule 16\.*

#### *Step 6: Remove Defender’s Casualties*

Remove the defender’s units that are behind the casualty strip from play. After casualties are removed, it might be necessary to re-evaluate certain units’ capabilities that depend on the presence of other units — for example, defending infantry might no longer be boosted by an artillery, or submarines might no longer have their abilities cancelled by an enemy destroyer. These changes take effect in the following combat round.

#### *Step 7: Press Attack or Retreat*

Combat rounds continue unless one of the following two conditions occurs, in this order:

**Condition A — Attacker and/or Defender Loses All Units.** Once all units that can either fire at a valid target or retreat on one or both sides have been destroyed, the combat ends. If a power has combat units remaining along the battle strip, that power wins the combat. In a sea battle, if both sides have only transports remaining, the attacker’s transports can remain in the contested sea zone or retreat.

**Condition B — Attacker Retreats.** The attacker (never the defender) can retreat during this step. Move all attacking land and sea units along the battle strip to a single adjacent friendly space from or through which at least 1 of the original attacking land or sea units moved. In the case of sea units, that space must have been friendly at the start of the turn. All such units must retreat together to the same space. **The destination must be within its stacking limit (Rule 28).**

Retreating air units remain in the contested space temporarily and complete their retreat movement during the Noncombat Move phase.

**Multinational Forces.** Units on the same side can share a territory or sea zone, constituting a multinational force. Such forces can defend together, but they can’t attack together, because each power moves and attacks with its own units only on its own turn. Any units in a sea zone belonging to an ally of the attacker (other than cargo on an attacker’s ship) can’t participate in the battle in any way.

An attacking fighter or tactical bomber can launch from an aircraft carrier owned by an ally, but the ally’s carrier can’t move until its owner’s turn. An attacking land unit can assault a coastal territory from an ally’s transport, but only on the turn of the attacking land unit’s owner.

**Transporting Multinational Forces** is a three-step process: you load your land units aboard the friendly transport on your turn; the transport’s owner moves it on that power’s turn; you offload your land units on your next turn.

#### *Step 8: Conclude Combat*

If you win a combat as the attacker in a territory and you have 1 or more surviving land units there, you take control of it. Otherwise it remains in the defender’s control. Sea units and air units can’t take control of a territory.

If you have captured the territory, place your control marker on it and adjust national production levels. Your national production increases by the value of the captured territory; the loser’s decreases by the same amount.

Any industrial complex, air base and/or naval base in the captured territory is now controlled by your side. If you capture an industrial complex, you can’t mobilize new units there until your next turn. If you capture a major industrial complex, it is immediately downgraded to a minor one. If you capture an air base or naval base, you can’t use the added movement or receive repairs until your next turn. Any damage previously inflicted remains until repaired.

**Stacking after combat.** If the surviving units in a captured or defended territory exceed its stacking limit (Rule 28), the owning player removes the excess units of their choice from play at the end of the Noncombat Move phase.

### **Liberating a Territory**

If you capture a territory that was originally controlled by another member of your side, you liberate it. You don’t take control; the original controller regains the territory and the national production level is adjusted. Any facilities revert to the original controller. A major industrial complex that was downgraded to a minor upon capture is not automatically upgraded upon liberation.

If the original controller’s capital is in enemy hands at the end of the turn in which you would otherwise have liberated the territory, you capture the territory instead.

### **Capturing and Liberating Capitals**

If a power captures a territory containing an enemy capital, follow the same rules as for capturing a territory. Add the captured territory’s income value to your national production level.

In addition, you collect all unspent IPCs from the treasury of the original controller of the captured capital (see also Rule 7, Capital Purge). You collect these IPCs even if your own capital is in enemy hands.

The original controller of a captured capital is still in the game but can’t collect income from any territories they still control and can’t buy new units. That player skips all but the Combat Move, Conduct Combat and Noncombat Move phases until the capital is liberated.

If a capital is liberated, the facilities in that capital territory revert to the original controller. Other territories and facilities originally controlled by the newly liberated capital’s controller but currently in the hands of friendly powers also revert control immediately.

You don’t collect IPCs from the controlling power when you liberate a capital.

Under the MOD ECR Victory Token System (Rule 2), capturing a capital does not end the game — it awards the corresponding victory token.

## **PHASE 5: NONCOMBAT MOVE**

In this phase you can move any of your units that didn’t move in the Combat Move phase or participate in combat during your turn. You will also land all your air units that participated in and survived the Conduct Combat phase.

Your land and sea units can move a number of spaces up to their move values. Your air units can move up to their move values, less the number of spaces they moved during the Combat Move phase. Only air units and submarines can move through hostile spaces during this phase.
